title: University of Oxford Entangles Multi-Species Atom Network and Extends Memory Storage Beyond 10 Seconds - Quantum Computing Report
gist: University of Oxford physicists built a trapped-ion quantum network that pairs strontium (88Sr+) network ions with calcium (43Ca+) memory ions, generating up to 4-qubit GHZ states across modules with ~92-97% fidelities. The calcium memory qubits held remote entanglement for over 10 seconds (τ = 14 ± 4 s), more than 100x the ~100 ms generation time, addressing a key hurdle for distributed quantum computing and sensing.

insights.claim: University of Oxford physicists demonstrated a heterogeneous trapped-ion quantum network that generates multipartite entangled states across separate modules using two atomic elements, strontium (88Sr+) and calcium (43Ca+), published in Physical Review Letters.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Modular, networked trapped-ion architectures are advancing as a scaling path for quantum computing.
insights.quote: physicists at the University of Oxford have demonstrated a heterogeneous quantum network that generates multipartite entangled states across separate trapped-ion modules using two distinct atomic elements

insights.claim: The Oxford team generated up to 4-qubit GHZ states distributed across trapped-ion modules, with the 4-qubit GHZ state reaching 91.90 ± 0.80% fidelity and Sr+–Sr+ Bell states reaching 96.94 ± 0.09% fidelity.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Fidelity benchmarks for distributed entanglement help gauge how close networked quantum hardware is to practical use.
insights.locator: Summary of Mixed-Species Remotely Entangled States

insights.claim: In the Oxford network, Sr+–Sr+ remote Bell-state generation had a 1.24% success probability and a 39.3 Hz net generation rate.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Low success probability and modest entanglement rates remain a throughput constraint for quantum networking.
insights.locator: Summary of Mixed-Species Remotely Entangled States

insights.claim: Distributed entanglement in the Oxford network was stored in calcium (43Ca+) memory qubits for more than 10 seconds (decay time constant τ = 14 ± 4 s), over 100x longer than the ~100 ms average entanglement generation time.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Long-lived quantum memory is a prerequisite for distributed quantum computing, so this removes a key technical bottleneck.
insights.quote: stored the distributed entanglement in calcium memory qubits for more than 10 seconds—extending entanglement lifetimes by more than 100x over the creation time

insights.claim: After 10 seconds of storage, the remotely entangled Ca+–Ca+ state's fidelity fell to 69.00 ± 4.00%, compared with 93.10 ± 0.70% for the freshly generated remote Ca+–Ca+ Bell state.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Fidelity degradation during storage shows long memory still trades off against state quality.
insights.locator: Summary of Mixed-Species Remotely Entangled States

insights.claim: The 43Ca+ hyperfine ground-state memory qubit is first-order insensitive to magnetic fields at 0.5 mT, about two orders of magnitude less sensitive than strontium, which is why it preserves entanglement so long.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Choice of atomic species for memory is a differentiating design lever for trapped-ion hardware developers.
insights.quote: the ground hyperfine manifold of 43Ca+ possesses first-order magnetic field insensitivity at 0.5 mT (~2 orders of magnitude lower sensitivity than strontium)

insights.claim: Preserving remote entanglement for over 10 seconds clears a major hurdle for both distributed quantum computing and quantum sensing networks, according to the article.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Signals progress toward networked quantum computing and sensing applications that could open new markets.
insights.quote: clearing a major hurdle for distributed quantum computing and quantum sensing networks

themes.theme: Why mixed species: separating networking from memory

insights.claim: Using a single atomic species for both photonic networking and quantum storage in trapped-ion networks creates a trade-off, because networking laser pulses and photon emissions cause decoherence and resonant light scattering in nearby memory qubits.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Explains why heterogeneous, mixed-species designs may become the architecture of choice for modular trapped-ion systems.
insights.quote: laser pulses and photon emissions required for networking induce decoherence and resonant light scattering in nearby memory qubits

insights.claim: Each Oxford network node co-traps one 88Sr+ ion as the optical network interface and one 43Ca+ ion as the memory qubit in microfabricated surface-electrode Paul traps; 422 nm photons from the strontium ions interfere at a central heralding station, and 402 nm Raman pulses transfer the entanglement to calcium via geometric phase gates and error-detected iSWAP operations.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Shows a concrete, microfabricated node design that could inform how commercial modular trapped-ion systems are engineered.
insights.quote: co-trapping one 88Sr+ ion (optical network interface) and one 43Ca+ ion (hyperfine ground memory qubit) in microfabricated surface-electrode Paul traps at each node
